sections.h2: Jo Daviess County at a glance
sections.html:
Jo Daviess County sits in the northwest corner of Illinois, with Galena as the county seat. Population is 21,594 and the county holds 13,535 housing units but only 10,391 households. A large share of homes are vacation or second homes, and 80.4 percent of occupied homes are owner-occupied. The median home value is $209,900 and median household income is $73,993. Residents 65 and older make up 31.5 percent of the population, so estate and downsizing sales are common here.

The second-home mix matters at tax time. Homestead relief goes only to full-time resident owners, so a buyer from out of state should not assume the seller's exemptions carry over.

Both main offices are in the County Courthouse at 330 North Bench Street, Galena. Hours are 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays, closed on holidays.

Jo Daviess County tax and assessment offices
OfficeLocation and phoneWhat it handles
County TreasurerSuite 149, 815-777-0355Prints and mails bills, collects tax, grants deferrals, runs the annual sale
Assessment OfficeSuite 1B, 815-777-1016Property records, exemptions, equalization, clerk to the Board of Review

The Assessment Office keeps the property record card for each parcel and tracks owners from deeds filed with the recorder. It mails a notice to any owner whose assessment changed. If you are unsure which township group covers your address, call before you list the house.

sections.h2: How the county collects real estate tax
sections.html:
The Treasurer also serves as County Collector and bills for roughly 110 local taxing bodies. After the bills go out, tax is payable in two installments. Whatever is still unpaid when the year ends goes into the annual tax sale, after the county publishes notice. Late installments pick up interest at 1 1/2 percent per month or part of a month, a rate the state sets for counties of this size (interest section of the Property Tax Code).

The county site has a free parcel search where you can reprint a bill. Payments can be made online through Govtech Services, and an owner can set up an individual escrow or advance payment there too. The Treasurer's forms page carries a deferral application, a direct deposit form and tax sale buyer registration forms. It also has hotel and motel use tax returns, so a lodging owner should confirm those are current before selling.

Ask the Treasurer for the installment dates tied to your own bill.

The county's rates span about 6.4554% to 11.21326%, and the median is 8.01228%. Where you land in that spread depends on the school, village, park and other districts your parcel sits in, and and those bodies, not the Assessment Office, set the rate. A homestead exemption lowers taxable value before the rate is applied, so the dollar savings depend on the parcel's rate. When you compare two houses, read the district list on each bill.

Complaints go to the Board of Review, which has three appointed members and convenes on or before the first Monday in June. Your complaint has to be written on the county's form and carry original signatures, because faxes are refused. The statute sets a window of 30 calendar days from publication of the assessment list (complaint section of the Property Tax Code).

Each township has its own filing window, announced in a local newspaper, and the Board cannot take a complaint after that window closes. Townships are split between The Galena Gazette and The Scoop for these notices, so ask the Assessment Office which paper carries yours and watch for the notice each spring.

Still unhappy after the Board rules? You can petition the Property Tax Appeal Board within 30 days of the written notice (appeal board section of the Property Tax Code). For reference, assessments outside Cook County are set at 33 1/3 percent of fair cash value (valuation section of the Property Tax Code).

sections.h2: Homestead exemptions and the residency rule
sections.html:
The Assessment Office administers these programs:

  • General homestead and homestead improvement.
  • Senior citizen homestead and senior citizen assessment freeze (PTAX-340).
  • Disabled persons (PTAX-343), disabled veteran (PTAX-342) and returning servicemember (PTAX-341) exemptions.
  • Disabled veteran standard exemption.

To qualify you must be a full-time county resident. When asked, show two of three documents: an Illinois driver's license, a federal tax return or an Illinois voter registration card, each listing the property address. Without two of the three, the homestead exemption is denied. Once bills have been printed, a missing renewal form for the low-income senior freeze, disabled person or disabled veteran exemption costs you that exemption for the year, with no exceptions.

Two more programs matter for an older house. The Treasurer's office runs the Senior Citizen Real Estate Tax Deferral Program, and applications are available after January 1. The Historic Freeze can hold the assessed value of an owner-occupied historic home for eight years, followed by a four-year step-up. It applies only after the state historic preservation office approves the rehabilitation, and the county starts the freeze only once it has that office's certificate.

sections.h2: What to bring to the office
sections.html: A short trip to the courthouse saves time. For the Treasurer, bring the parcel number or the property address and your most recent bill, plus the lender's name if the tax is escrowed. For the Assessment Office, bring your deed or closing statement, the last assessment notice, and any exemption renewal forms you received in the mail. If you are asking about a deferral, bring the application you picked up after January 1. Staff can usually tell you on the spot whether a parcel sits in a township group with a filing window still open.

Work through this list before you sign the contract:

  • Pull the parcel from the county's free property search and compare it with your last bill.
  • Confirm which township group assesses the parcel.
  • Find out whether a deferral lien, a historic freeze or an exemption renewal is pending.
  • If a lender escrows your tax, ask it for the year's payment history.
  • Tell the title company about any lodging or short-term rental activity, since hotel and motel returns are filed with the Treasurer.

Your contract should say who pays the bill that arrives after closing and how the year is split, so the buyer's first bill holds no surprise. If the house is a parent's estate, pull the exemption and deferral records early. A deferral lien will show up in the buyer's title search and has to be cleared at closing.

A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, which helps when an old house has tax or record questions still open. Even then, the tax bill and any lien are settled from the proceeds at the closing table.

faqs.q: Is Jo Daviess County property tax paid in two parts?
faqs.a: Yes. Real estate tax is payable in two installments after the bills are mailed. Ask the Treasurer for the dates printed on your bill.

faqs.q: Can I still file an assessment appeal this year?
faqs.a: Only if your township window is open. The Board of Review cannot take complaints after the filing date, so call the Assessment Office at 815-777-1016 to confirm where your township stands.

faqs.q: What proof of residency does the county require for exemptions?
faqs.a: Two of three documents: an Illinois driver's license, a federal tax return or an Illinois voter registration card, each showing the property address.

faqs.q: Who do I call about my assessment?
faqs.a: Call the township assessor for the township where the home sits, or the county Assessment Office at 815-777-1016.

faqs.q: Does the county offer a tax deferral for seniors?
faqs.a: Yes. The Treasurer reviews and grants deferrals, and the application is available from that office after January 1 each year. Call 815-777-0355.
